summary: Carbazochrome (an oxidation product of adrenaline, used as the sodium sulfonate or salicylate salt) is a haemostatic agent that works by reducing increased capillary permeability and fragility. It is NOT approved by the US FDA and is used mainly in Japan, other parts of Asia, and some European countries; the information here is therefore based on regional product literature and pharmacology rather than an FDA label. It is used for the prevention and treatment of capillary bleeding - such as epistaxis, retinal and renal haemorrhage, purpura, and oozing during or after surgery and dental procedures. Importantly, carbazochrome stabilises the capillary wall and does NOT act on the coagulation cascade, platelet number, or function, so it is ineffective for bleeding from large vessels or coagulation defects and is not a substitute for definitive haemostasis or correction of a coagulopathy. It is generally well tolerated, and robust clinical-efficacy evidence is limited; it is frequently used as a combination ingredient.
indications: Prevention and treatment of capillary bleeding due to increased capillary permeability/fragility - e.g. epistaxis, retinal haemorrhage, renal/urinary bleeding, purpura, and intra- or post-operative oozing (per regional product labelling; not an FDA-approved indication)

moa: Carbazochrome is an oxidation product of adrenaline (adrenochrome) formulated as a stable, water-soluble salt (sodium sulfonate or salicylate). It exerts a haemostatic effect by reducing the increased permeability and fragility of capillaries, thereby strengthening the capillary wall and decreasing capillary bleeding. It is thought to act on the capillary endothelium and surrounding connective tissue rather than on the plasma coagulation factors. Crucially, it does not alter prothrombin time, platelet count, or platelet function and has no effect on the coagulation cascade, so its action is limited to capillary-level bleeding from increased vascular permeability.

preg: There are limited data on carbazochrome in pregnancy. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed and after weighing the limited evidence of benefit against unknown risks.
lact: There are limited data on carbazochrome during breastfeeding. Use only if clearly needed.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is established. Use with general caution; there are no robust data in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is established. Use with general caution; there are no robust data in significant hepatic impairment.

pearls: Carbazochrome is NOT FDA-approved; it is used in Japan/Asia and parts of Europe - this record is based on regional product literature, not an FDA label.
It is a capillary-stabilising haemostatic that reduces capillary permeability and fragility; it does NOT act on the coagulation cascade, platelets, or clotting times.
Because it works only at the capillary level, it is ineffective for bleeding from coagulation defects or large vessels and must not delay definitive haemostasis.
It is derived from adrenochrome (an oxidation product of adrenaline) but has no significant sympathomimetic activity.
It is light-sensitive (store protected from light) and is often used as a combination haemostatic ingredient.
High-quality efficacy evidence is limited; use as an adjunct rather than primary therapy for significant bleeding.
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered, or skip it if it is almost time for the next dose - do not take a double dose. If it was prescribed for active bleeding, follow your clinician's specific instructions.
overdose: Carbazochrome has low acute toxicity and there is little information on overdose. Excessive doses would most likely cause gastrointestinal upset. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive and symptomatic. With combination products, consider and manage the effects of any co-ingredients (e.g. salicylate from a salicylate salt).
